headline: Payrolls 29,000. Yields rose anyway.
standfirst: Friday's September jobs report did what a week of Fed speeches had already half done: payrolls rose 29,000 against about 90,000 expected, July and August were cut by a net 60,000, unemployment rose to 4.2% and hourly earnings rose 0.1% on the month, 3.0% on the year, the slowest since May 2021. October's hike went to about 22% priced from 64% a week earlier, and the Nasdaq touched a record, with the Nasdaq Composite up 1.19% to 27,190.86, the S&P 500 up 0.73% to 7,722.72 and the Dow up 0.49% to 51,176.96. Treasuries did not join in: the ten-year closed near 5.27%, about 3bp higher, after Dallas Fed President Logan said rates need to rise another half point, and it ended the week about 11bp higher, a few basis points below Thursday's 5.344% high, the highest since 2002. Crude eased on a G7 stock release, unchanged OPEC+ quotas and Gulf exports above pre-war levels, but Iran says Hormuz stays closed until its plan is accepted and a third US carrier group is heading for the region. Euro-area inflation printed 3.8%, the euro is near its lowest since May 2025, and Tokyo core CPI printed 2.7%. Asia is higher, the Nikkei about 2% near 69,700 and Taiwan 2.5%, with mainland China and Korea shut. Today: ISM services at 10:00 ET. This week: Williams and Bowman, three coupon auctions and the FOMC minutes.

bullets.title: Jobs: a 29,000 print, a 60,000 downward revision, October hike at about 22% — and a Fed that did not call it over
bullets.text: Nonfarm payrolls rose 29,000 against 90,000 in the Bloomberg survey and 84,000 in others; August was revised to 133,000 from 162,000 and July to a loss of 10,000 from a gain of 21,000, a net 60,000 fewer jobs, and the three-month average is near 51,000. Private payrolls rose 46,000 against about 81,000 expected, led by health care at 23,000 and leisure and hospitality at 10,000. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2% from 4.1% with participation up to 61.8% from 61.6% and the labour force larger, so part of the rise is entrants rather than layoffs; U6 slipped to 7.6%. Average hourly earnings rose 0.1% against 0.3% expected and 3.0% on the year, the slowest since May 2021. Factory orders rose 0.1% as expected. Futures put an October hike at about 22%, from 64% a week earlier and a brief 13% low on Friday; December is the favoured date and roughly two more moves are priced for the first half of 2027. Jefferies' Thomas Simons called it the nail in the coffin for October. The Fed speakers did not: Logan said the range needs another 50bp while noting higher yields are doing some of the tightening, Goolsbee that every option is on the table and inflation is the larger concern, Hammack and Mester that there is time before the 27–28 October meeting, and Fifth Third's Bill Adams that September CPI, PPI, oil and geopolitics are likelier to decide it than this report. CPI is on 14 October.

bullets.title: Rates and the dollar: yields fell for minutes, then closed higher; the dollar is at a 17-month high
bullets.text: Treasury yields dropped on the report and reversed within hours as Logan spoke. The ten-year closed near 5.27%, about 3bp higher on the day and 11bp higher on the week, and the two-year near 4.82%, up about 3bp on the day and down about 3bp on the week; early Monday they are near 5.26% and 4.81%. The ten-year touched 5.344% on Thursday, its highest since 2002, and the thirty-year 5.642% on Wednesday. Standard Chartered's Cedric Lam says forced selling by hedge funds and property trusts is delaying a move lower, mortgage rates are reported near 7.5%, and the long Treasury ETF fell 0.30% on Friday and is down 5.75% over a month. The dollar index is about 102, a third straight weekly gain and the highest in 17 months. The euro is near $1.12, its lowest since May 2025 after four weekly declines: France's public debt is reported at 119% of output, its 2027 budget needs 54 billion euros of savings from a parliament with no majority for them, and its ten-year yield touched the highest since 2002 last week. Friday's euro-area flash inflation of 3.8%, a three-year high with energy at 18.8% and core 2.5%, was above the 3.6–3.7% expected, and Standard Chartered still expects the ECB to wait for December's projections on 29 October. Tokyo core CPI printed 2.7% against 2.3–2.4% expected with the core-core measure at 3.0%; some economists, among them Sompo's Koike, now expect the Bank of Japan to move in October, while most investors look to December. USD/JPY is 158.0.

bullets.title: Equities: a Nasdaq record on a weak jobs report, a bounce in Europe, and Asia chasing it with China and Korea shut
bullets.text: Friday's gains were broad: every sector but health care rose, led by consumer discretionary at 1.13% and technology at 1.01%, the Philadelphia semiconductor index gained 2.40% and 3.69% on the week, Nvidia touched a record $237.88, ON Semiconductor rose about 6.5% on a revised Synaptics deal, and the Russell 2000 gained 0.94%, its best day in nearly a month. Western Digital and Seagate fell about 10% after a report that Toshiba will double hard-drive capacity; Nike fell about 10% premarket after Thursday's guidance cut and pared much of it. The VIX closed at 15.31. For the week the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.5%, a third straight gain, while the S&P 500 fell 0.3% and the Dow 1.3%; the S&P 500 is up about 13% this year and about 1% below its mid-August record. Europe rebounded 0.75% on the Stoxx 600 to 631.35, a day after a four-month low, and is 1.1% lower on the week; Germany is reported to be raising its 2026 growth forecast to 1.3% from 0.5%. In Asia the Nikkei is up about 2% near 69,700 after trading above 70,000, Taiwan up about 2.5% and Hong Kong flat after Friday's 2.6% fall, its biggest since 23 March; mainland China is closed until 8 October and Korea today. The fourth-quarter earnings season opens with PepsiCo on Thursday and Delta on Friday, then the banks on the 13th.

bullets.title: Oil and Iran: a stock release and rising exports against a closed strait, a third carrier group and attacks on Saudi sites
bullets.text: December Brent is $101.73 and WTI $90.07, down 0.51% and 1.14%; Friday's settlements were about $91.55 for WTI, down 1.4%, and about $102.6–102.8 for Brent. The G7 agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of crude and diesel from emergency stocks through the IEA and to avoid export restrictions after pressure from Washington; the top OPEC+ producers left November production targets unchanged; and Kpler counts Middle East crude exports above their pre-war average of about 18 million barrels a day on several days in late September, with a seven-day average of 18.5 million on 1 October and refined-product shipments still near half of pre-war. Against that, Iran's chief negotiator Ghalibaf said on Sunday that Hormuz stays closed until the US accepts Tehran's seven-day plan, the UK maritime agency reports at least one attack a day in the strait or the Gulf of Aden since 2 October, the Houthis claimed missile and drone strikes on Aramco sites near Riyadh that started a large fire, Saudi Arabia is reported to be planning an offensive against them, Iran's oil minister resigned amid fuel queues, and the US is moving the Theodore Roosevelt carrier group and the Makin Island amphibious group, about 9,000 people, towards the region for arrival around the end of October, which would make three carriers. The US also pulled bombers from RAF Fairford after the UK linked a terror plot to Iran, and Trump said Iran would have to choose the easy way or the hard way. Brent's weekly and monthly columns still straddle Wednesday's November expiry. Gold is $4,162, down 7% over a month; sugar rose 5.23% and cocoa 5.37% on Friday.

bullets.title: Today and the week: ISM services, Williams, three auctions, the FOMC minutes, then Michigan
bullets.text: Monday: ISM services at 10:00 ET seen 55.2–55.7 after 55.4 with prices paid after 72.6, alongside the final S&P Global US composite PMI at 09:45, seen 58.4; euro-area, UK and German services PMIs earlier; mainland China closed until 8 October and Korea today. Tuesday: euro-area retail sales at 05:00 ET; Williams at 09:05 ET and Bowman at 10:45; the three-year note auction at 13:00; Lamb Weston and RPM. Wednesday: Constellation Brands before the open; the ten-year note auction at 13:00 ET; the minutes of the 16 September meeting at 14:00, which should show how many of the twelve wanted a faster path; Levi Strauss after the close. Thursday: the ECB's account of its 10 September meeting at 07:30 ET; jobless claims at 08:30 seen 195,000; PepsiCo before the open; the thirty-year bond auction at 13:00; Musalem at 13:40. Friday: Canada's jobs report at 08:30 ET seen 6.5% unemployment; Michigan sentiment, preliminary, at 10:00, seen 48.1 with one-year inflation expectations last at 4.6%; Delta reports. The bond market is shut on Monday 12 October for Columbus Day, with Hammack speaking that afternoon. Then the RBA minutes and German final inflation on the 13th with JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo and Citigroup reporting, China CPI, US CPI and the Beige Book on the 14th, US retail sales and PPI on the 15th, China's third-quarter GDP on the 16th, UK labour data on the 20th, UK CPI on the 21st and the flash PMIs on the 23rd, with the FOMC on 27–28 October.

calendar.event: ISM services (September); S&P Global composite PMI, final 09:45
calendar.note: Seen 55.2–55.7 after 55.4, with prices paid after 72.6. Manufacturing prices paid jumped to 77.9 last Thursday; services is where the energy shock shows up second. The first full session after payrolls.
Williams' 'no need for urgency' on 29 September began the October repricing and he expects one more hike this year. Bowman is a voter; neither has spoken since payrolls.
The first coupon supply since the ten-year touched 5.344%. The last three-year cleared at 4.474%; the two-year is 4.83% now.
The week's test of term premium: the last ten-year cleared at 4.834%, and the benchmark is about 45bp higher. Supply, not the Fed, has been what moved the long end.
The record of the 12–0 hike. Watch how many wanted a faster path and whether 'no need for urgency' was already the centre of the committee, now that October is about 22% priced.
The accounts of 10 September land after euro-area inflation printed 3.8% and before the 29 October meeting. Claims are seen near 195,000 after 197,000.

calendar.event: 30-year bond auction; PepsiCo before the open
calendar.note: The long bond touched 5.642% last Wednesday, its highest since 2002, and Barclays talks about 6%. The last auction cleared at 5.308%. PepsiCo is the first big staples report of the quarter.
Seen 48.1, the series low last month, with one-year inflation expectations at 4.6%. Canada's jobs report is at 08:30 ET and Delta reports. The bond market is shut on Monday 12th.

sessionNote: A normal Monday after an abnormal Friday. Asia has rallied on the Nasdaq record while mainland China and Korea are shut, so the moves in Tokyo and Taipei are thin-liquidity moves. Europe opens with the euro near $1.12, French spreads and the 3.8% inflation print to digest, and the ECB's October meeting back in question. The US session has one scheduled catalyst before the afternoon: ISM services at 10:00 ET, read through its prices-paid line, with Williams and Bowman tomorrow and the three-year auction at 13:00. The pattern Friday set is the one to watch: the front end priced the soft data at 08:30 ET, the ten-year gave it back by lunchtime on a Fed speaker, and the close was higher in yield. A repeat on ISM prices would say the market is pricing supply and inflation, not the October meeting. Oil is the weekend's other signal: December Brent near $101.7 with Hormuz, Fairford and a third carrier group in the headlines, and the G7 release and Gulf exports pulling the other way. The brief, the map and the calendar hold until tomorrow's refresh.
watchOut: Reading Friday as the end of the hiking cycle. October is about 22% priced, not zero; December is the favoured date, two more moves are priced for the first half of 2027, Logan wants half a point and the ten-year closed higher on payrolls day. The report itself is softer in the detail than the headline: 60,000 of the miss is revisions to earlier months, unemployment rose partly because participation rose, and the Fed has said that wage growth is not what it is worried about. September CPI on 14 October, with energy running at 18.8% inflation in the euro area and manufacturing prices paid at 77.9, is the print that decides whether payrolls mattered. Second, thin Asia: with mainland China and Korea closed, a 2% Nikkei is a lighter signal than it looks. Third, the Brent columns: five-day and one-month changes still straddle the November expiry, and Friday's Brent 'week' compares the new contract with the old. Size for a two-way ISM at 10:00 ET and a Fed-speaker reversal, and read the auctions, not the headline, for the long end.

archive.headline: Core PCE 3.0%. Bonds' worst month since 2022.
archive.summary: Core PCE printed 3.0% against 3.3% after the BEA's annual revision rewrote July, ADP beat at 90,000, final Q2 GDP was revised up to 2.2% and Chicago PMI jumped to 58.8; October's hike odds slid to 35–40% while the ten-year and thirty-year rose again to close a September in which the ten-year added about 50bp, its worst month since 2022. Micron beat and guided above consensus; the November Brent contract expired at $103.53; the Nikkei rose 3.24%.

archive.headline: October hike back to a coin flip.
archive.summary: Job openings fell to a five-month low, consumer confidence to a 2014 low and Williams said there was 'no need for urgency', taking October's hike from about 70% to about 50% priced; the two-year fell 6bp while the thirty-year touched 5.621%, its highest since 2002. Brent settled 2.6% lower on recovering Saudi exports, Australia's CPI printed 4.0% and the Aussie fell through 70 cents.

archive.headline: The ten-year closed at 5.24%. Nothing else mattered.
archive.summary: The ten-year closed at 5.236%, its highest since 2007, and the S&P 500 fell 0.77% to a ten-session low as Trump's rejection of Iran's Hormuz offer put Brent back above $107; Cook and Barkin talked rates higher, gold fell 3% to a seven-week low, and the RBA hiked to 4.60% overnight. The November Brent roll and Washington's reply to Tehran via Qatar were the day's traps.

archive.headline: Trump said no. Oil is back above $107.
archive.summary: Trump rejected Iran's seven-day Hormuz offer over the weekend and Brent recovered Friday's fall before New York opened; gold fell to its lowest since early August, the Kospi lost 2.5% and the dollar hit a two-month high. The front end eased with October's hike odds while the long end kept rising, into a week of PCE, ISM and payrolls.

archive.headline: The week the Treasury market stopped waiting for the Fed
archive.summary: Weekend edition. The ten-year went from 4.95% to 5.21% in a week on a 58.4 flash PMI, three auctions at two-decade highs and eight Fed speakers, and every Treasury from two years out cleared 5%. Equities held on Meta and AMD while the Dow fell for a fourth week, Brent round-tripped $100–$99–$106 on Iran, and October was 71% priced for a second hike.
